lessons.title: Understanding N-P-K and Micronutrients
lessons.body: Tomatoes need 16 nutrients to grow well. The three main ones are Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), and Potassium (K). These are the numbers you see on fertilizer bags, like 20-10-20. Nitrogen makes leaves and stems grow strong and green. Phosphorus helps roots and flowers form. Potassium makes fruit grow big, red, and sweet. When you buy fertilizer, look for a blend made for tomatoes. In Africa, common fertilizers include DAP (18-46-0) for planting, and CAN (27% N) for top dressing. But tomatoes also need small amounts of micronutrients: calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc, boron, and others. Without them, you get problems like blossom end rot (calcium) or yellow leaves (magnesium). A simple way to supply micronutrients is to add well-rotted manure or compost. You can also buy micronutrient mixes at agro-dealers. Test your soil first. In many African soils, nitrogen is low, phosphorus is often low, and potassium is medium. But don't guess. A soil test costs little and saves money. For a 10 by 10 meter plot, you might need 2 kg of DAP at planting and 1 kg of CAN when fruits start forming. Always follow label instructions. Over-fertilizing wastes money and harms plants. Remember: N-P-K is the foundation, but micronutrients are the fine-tuning.

lessons.title: Side-Dressing and Fertigation Techniques
lessons.body: Side-dressing means adding fertilizer to the soil beside growing plants. It gives tomatoes a boost when they need it most. The first side-dress is when the first flowers appear. Use 1 tablespoon of CAN (calcium ammonium nitrate) per plant, placed 10 cm from the stem. Cover with soil and water. The second side-dress is when fruits are swelling. Use 1 tablespoon of a balanced fertilizer like 17-17-17. Never put fertilizer directly on the stem; it burns. For larger farms, you can use a hoe to make a small furrow between rows and sprinkle fertilizer, then cover. Fertigation is mixing fertilizer into irrigation water. It saves labor and gives nutrients directly to roots. You can use a bucket and watering can for small plots. Mix 1 teaspoon of water-soluble fertilizer (like 20-20-20) per liter of water. Apply 1 liter per plant every week. For drip irrigation, use a venturi injector. Common in Kenya and South Africa, these cost about $50. Always flush the lines with plain water after fertigation to prevent clogging. If you use organic methods, you can fertigate with compost tea. Dilute 1 part tea to 5 parts water. Apply every 2 weeks. Both methods work best when soil is moist. Never fertigate dry soil; it can burn roots. Also, avoid side-dressing when heavy rain is expected, as nutrients wash away.

lessons.title: Organic Fertilizers: Compost Tea, Manure, and More
lessons.body: Organic fertilizers feed both plants and soil. They are cheap and locally available. Compost tea is made by soaking compost in water. Put 1 part compost in 5 parts water in a bucket. Stir daily for 3 days. Strain and spray on leaves or pour around roots. It adds nutrients and beneficial microbes. Manure is another option. Use only well-rotted manure, at least 6 months old. Fresh manure burns plants and carries weeds. Apply 2-3 kg per square meter before planting. Poultry manure is rich in nitrogen; cow manure is milder. You can also use kitchen scraps, banana peels, and eggshells. Bury them near plants. Wood ash is a good source of potassium and calcium. Sprinkle a handful around each plant, but not too close to the stem. Bone meal adds phosphorus. Blood meal adds nitrogen. In Africa, you can find these at agro-dealers or make your own. For liquid fertilizer, soak manure in water for a week (1 part manure to 10 parts water). Use the liquid to water plants. Organic fertilizers release nutrients slowly, so apply them early. They also improve soil structure, helping sandy soils hold water and clay soils drain. Combine organics with small amounts of mineral fertilizers for best results. This is called integrated soil fertility management. It is the best approach for African smallholders.

lessons.title: Recognizing and Correcting Nutrient Deficiencies
lessons.body: Tomato leaves tell you what nutrients are missing. Nitrogen deficiency: older leaves turn yellow, then whole plant is pale and stunted. Fix: side-dress with CAN or urea (1 tablespoon per plant) or spray with compost tea. Phosphorus deficiency: leaves turn dark green with purple tints, especially on undersides. Plants are stunted. Fix: apply DAP or bone meal. Potassium deficiency: leaf edges turn yellow and brown, starting on older leaves. Fruit is small and uneven. Fix: apply wood ash or potassium sulfate. Calcium deficiency: blossom end rot â a black, sunken spot on the bottom of fruit. Fix: spray with calcium chloride (1 teaspoon per liter) or add gypsum to soil. Magnesium deficiency: older leaves have yellow patches between green veins. Fix: spray with Epsom salts (1 tablespoon per liter). Iron deficiency: young leaves turn yellow with green veins. Fix: spray with chelated iron. Zinc deficiency: small leaves, short internodes. Fix: spray with zinc sulfate. Boron deficiency: brittle stems, hollow fruit. Fix: apply borax very sparingly (1 teaspoon per 10 square meters). Always confirm by checking multiple plants. Sometimes symptoms are due to drought or disease, not nutrient lack. Correct deficiencies quickly with foliar sprays, which act in 2-3 days. Soil applications take 1-2 weeks. Keep a notebook to track what you see and what you apply.

lessons.title: Foliar Feeding for Quick Nutrient Uptake
lessons.body: Foliar feeding means spraying liquid fertilizer directly on leaves. Plants absorb nutrients through their leaves faster than through roots. This is useful when plants show deficiency symptoms or during critical stages like flowering and fruiting. To foliar feed, use a knapsack sprayer or a simple hand sprayer. Mix water-soluble fertilizer according to label. For a general boost, use 20-20-20 at 1 teaspoon per liter. For calcium, use calcium nitrate at 1 teaspoon per liter. For magnesium, use Epsom salts at 1 tablespoon per liter. Spray early morning or late evening to avoid leaf burn from sun. Spray the undersides of leaves too, where pores are. Add a few drops of liquid soap to help the spray stick. Do not spray in strong wind or before rain. Repeat every 7-10 days until symptoms improve. For organic options, use compost tea or seaweed extract (1 part to 10 parts water). Seaweed extract is sold in many African agro-shops and contains growth hormones. Foliar feeding is not a replacement for soil fertilization. It is a supplement. Use it when roots cannot take up enough nutrients, like in waterlogged or very dry soil. Also, do not overdo it. Too much foliar feed can burn leaves. Always test on a few plants first. Keep records of what you spray and when.

lessons.title: Avoiding Fertilizer Burn and Over-Fertilization
lessons.body: Fertilizer burn happens when too much fertilizer touches roots or leaves. Symptoms include yellowing, wilting, and brown, scorched leaf edges. The plant may die. Over-fertilization also causes lush green leaves but few fruits, and it wastes money. To avoid burn, always follow recommended rates. For example, a common recommendation for tomatoes is 2 kg of DAP per 100 square meters at planting. Do not exceed this. When side-dressing, keep fertilizer 10 cm from the stem. Water the soil before and after applying fertilizer. Never apply fertilizer to dry soil. For foliar sprays, do not exceed 1 tablespoon per liter for most nutrients. If you see burn, flush the soil with plenty of water to wash away excess salts. This may take several days. For foliar burn, rinse leaves with plain water. To prevent over-fertilization, test your soil. In many African soils, you may only need nitrogen and phosphorus. Adding potassium when it is already high is a waste. Also, rotate crops. Tomatoes follow legumes like beans or groundnuts, which add nitrogen. Use organic matter to improve soil slowly. Remember, more fertilizer is not better. It is about balance. Keep a calendar of when you apply what. If you are unsure, apply half the recommended rate and see how plants respond.

quiz.q: What do the numbers on a fertilizer bag represent?
quiz.explanation: The numbers show the percentage of Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most important for fruit development and sweetness?
quiz.explanation: Potassium is key for fruit size, color, and sugar content.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is commonly used for planting tomatoes in Africa?
quiz.explanation: DAP (18-46-0) is high in phosphorus, good for root development at planting.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of calcium deficiency in tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Calcium deficiency causes blossom end rot, a black spot on the fruit bottom.

quiz.q: How much CAN should you apply per plant when side-dressing?
quiz.explanation: One tablespoon of CAN per plant is a common side-dress rate.

quiz.q: What is fertigation?
options: B) Mixing fertilizer with irrigation water
quiz.explanation: Fertigation is the application of fertilizer through an irrigation system.

quiz.q: Which organic fertilizer is rich in nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Poultry manure has high nitrogen content compared to other manures.

quiz.q: How long should manure be aged before use?
quiz.explanation: Well-rotted manure should be at least 6 months old to avoid burning plants.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of nitrogen deficiency in tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen is mobile, so deficiency shows first on older leaves as yellowing.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes yellowing between green veins on older leaves?
quiz.explanation: Magnesium deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis on older leaves.

quiz.q: What is a quick fix for iron deficiency?
quiz.explanation: Chelated iron foliar spray provides quickly available iron.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes hollow fruit?
quiz.explanation: Boron deficiency can lead to hollow or cracked fruit.

quiz.q: What is the best time to foliar feed?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Spraying in cooler times prevents leaf burn and improves absorption.

quiz.q: How much Epsom salts per liter for magnesium foliar spray?
quiz.explanation: One tablespoon of Epsom salts per liter is a standard foliar rate.

quiz.q: What can you add to foliar spray to help it stick?
quiz.explanation: A few drops of liquid soap act as a surfactant to spread and stick.

quiz.q: How often should you repeat foliar feeding until symptoms improve?
quiz.explanation: Repeat every 7-10 days for best results without over-fertilizing.

quiz.q: What is a sign of fertilizer burn?
options: A) Yellow leaves with green veins
quiz.explanation: Fertilizer burn causes leaf edges to turn brown and scorched.

quiz.q: How can you correct fertilizer burn?
quiz.explanation: Flushing with water leaches excess salts away from roots.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake that leads to over-fertilization?
quiz.explanation: Guessing without a soil test often leads to too much fertilizer.

quiz.q: Which crop rotation can reduce nitrogen need for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Legumes like beans fix nitrogen, making it available for the next crop.

quiz.q: What is the recommended distance from the stem when side-dressing?
quiz.explanation: Placing fertilizer 10 cm from the stem prevents root burn.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is high in phosphorus?
quiz.explanation: DAP (18-46-0) is high in phosphorus, essential for root growth.

quiz.q: What is compost tea?
options: C) A type of fertilizer granule
quiz.explanation: Compost tea is made by soaking compost in water to extract nutrients.

quiz.q: How much water should you mix with 1 part compost for compost tea?
quiz.explanation: A 1:5 ratio of compost to water is common for compost tea.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is supplied by wood ash?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is a good source of potassium and calcium.

quiz.q: What is integrated soil fertility management?
options: B) Combining organic and mineral fertilizers
quiz.explanation: It combines organic and mineral inputs for best soil health and yields.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes small leaves and short internodes?
quiz.explanation: Zinc deficiency leads to little leaf and shortened internodes.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of calcium chloride for foliar spray?
quiz.explanation: One teaspoon per liter is a safe rate for calcium foliar spray.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid foliar feeding in strong wind?
options: C) It drifts and misses plants
quiz.explanation: Wind causes spray drift, reducing effectiveness and wasting product.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are unsure about fertilizer rate?
quiz.explanation: Applying half the recommended rate and observing plant response is safer.
